DEADLY DELIVERANCE

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
He went in for healing. He left in a body bag.

Unique Selling Point:
We investigate a Christian recovery centre where the Bible is weaponised against addicts seeking rehabilitation and repentance.

Summary:
Luke Edwards was 32. A writer. A chess player. A son. And in the grip of a cannabis-induced psychosis in April this year when his family made the call: send him to a Christian rehab centre on the KZN South Coast - a place that promised healing through prayer.
Nine days later, Luke’s body was found - barefoot, shirtless, and dumped in the bushes (in full display for the world to see) near a retirement home. He’d been beaten so badly, investigators said it looked like torture.
The Tetelestai Recovery Centre said he’d “absconded.” But CCTV tells another story…

Hours after his supposed escape, Luke is caught on camera - fully clothed, calm, coherent, and very much alive.
Witnesses say he was cable-tied, locked in a holding cell at the facility, and beaten for days by so-called “monitors” - ex-addicts turned enforcers.
Not staff. Not trained. Just violent men recruited for muscle, not mercy.
And the facility? No doctors. No therapists. No psychiatric oversight. Just scripture, fear, and fists.

TRC’s founder, Donovan de Klerk, once hailed as a “_Young Mandela_,” now faces a different spotlight.
Since Luke’s death:
- Four residents have been charged with murder (as of yesterday).
- Three staff members face assault and intimidation charges.
- One resident has died by suicide (a week after Luke’s death).
- Another was hospitalised and is in ICU after allegedly being beaten for defending a witness.

According to Luke’s family, this wasn’t recovery, this was murder.

Luke Edwards is one name, but witnesses say he’s not the first.




Further information:
We investigate a Christian rehab centre where salvation came at the end of a fist, and how South Africa’s faith-based facilities are operating in the shadows, trading therapy for theology, and with no rules, no oversight, and no accountability.
And we expose what really happened in the final hours of Luke Edwards’ life - through the eyes of witnesses, a veteran PI hired by his grieving family to uncover the truth; and CCTV footage.


Extra Budget Items:
Shooting required in both Cape Town and Durban

Press Release:


Deadly Deliverance

A young man in the grip of cannabis-induced psychosis is admitted to a Christian rehab centre on the KwaZulu Natal coast. Days later, his body is found
barefoot, shirtless, and beaten so badly, it looks like torture. Witnesses provide shocking accounts, and investigations reveal the centre has no doctors, no therapists, and no psychiatric oversight. What really happened to this young man inside the facility,
which promised healing through prayer? His family believes he was murdered… and witnesses claim he’s not the first.

Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


DEADLY DELIVERANCE: FINAL
(MASA): “It’s early morning in April this year.
(MASA): “CCTV footage shows a young man probably disoriented, possibly Injured.”
(MASA): “It’s later established that he’s an escapee from a nearby drug rehabilitation centre.”
(MASA): “Hours later… Luke Edwards is found dead.”
(MASA): “The centre in question promised healing through Christian scripture... but insiders reveal its methods were anything but spiritual.”
(PATIENT 1 - ANONYMOUS): “They told us pain was part of the process. That suffering meant we were healing.”
(MASA): “Punishment was routine.”
(PATIENT 2 - ANONYMOUS): “He uses punishment as a form of - if you abide to this punishment, God will forgive you.”
(MASA): “Luke died less than a week after being admitted.”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “I can tell that this man was beaten for a long period of time.”
(LINDA DAVIDS): “They were beating psychosis out of people… and that’s why he’s dead.”
(MASA): “The centre’s name comes from the Bible. Tetelestai means: “It is finished.”

(MASA): “For Luke… it was.”


(MASA): “Luke had just returned from abroad. He was 32. A writer.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “He was clever, he was artistic, he was passionate about things. He had friends all over the world. He loved like I’ve never seen a boy love.”
(MASA): “But, after his return, he became paranoid... agitated. His family was told he was experiencing cannabis-induced psychosis.”

(MASA): “Searching for help, they found Tetelestai Recovery Centre in Amanzimtoti, in KZN.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “So we went out to the centre. We had a long meeting with him.”
(MASA): “Luke’s parents, Linda and Duncan Edwards, with the founder, Donovan de Klerk.”

(MASA): “He assured them Luke would be evaluated by a doctor.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “I said to him: ‘Do you have a psychiatrist or a psychologist on the premises?’; he said no they don’t, but they have a doctor that comes in once a week, and she’ll do a full evaluation; if she feels he needs to go to a psychiatrist, they will.”
(MASA): “Reassured, they had Luke admitted.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “He had I think a two-week initial period there where they detox and they're not allowed to see family and that, I said that’s fine. I said after that, I will get my own psychiatrist in there to check on Luke, and he said that wasn’t a problem’.”
(MASA): “So it didn’t even get to two weeks?”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “No, no, no. Within a, well literally a week, the following Tuesday he was dead.”


(MASA): “Tetelestai told the family Luke had escaped the facility the night before he was found.”
(MASA): “They didn’t immediately phone the police… or his parents.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “If they had phoned me at 11 o’clock that night, we family would never let Luke wander around at 11 o’clock night…”
(DUNCAN EDWARDS): “I still would’ve been there…”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “We would’ve been there at 11 o’ clock and maybe we could’ve saved Luke…”
(MASA): “Now you were given a version of events by the centre of what had happened initially… Does that information contradict one another?”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “Oh absolutely. Absolutely…”
(MASA): “Tell me how…?”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “They say he absconded, so for me he escaped. From witnesses that have - he was actually pushed ou himself.”
(DUNCAN EDWARDS): “Dragged out.”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “He was dragged out.”
(MASA): “Luke’s lifeless body was found somewhere around here - in the street, just 250 metres away from Tetelestai’s gates.”
(MASA): “Four men from the centre were charged with his murder. They weren’t trained staff. Just former addicts who’d finished the programme. Tetelestai called them “monitors.”
(MASA): “Were you told about the monitors when you spoke to Donovan initially?”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “Nope… As far as we were aware, all his employees had the right qualifications.”
(MASA): “Luke’s injuries were extensive: bruises, blunt force trauma, cable tie marks, and a knife wound believed to be fatal.”
(DUNCAN EDWARDS): “I went to the morgue. I saw his body. It was the most horrific thing I’ve ever seen in my entire life. Worst day of my life. I went there with my brother-in-laws, and we just all - we were mortified at the condition his body was in. It was, it was mind blowing. Absolutely mind blowing.”

(MASA): “What Tetelestai offers isn’t recognised therapy. It’s a religious belief system which is built on a model called ‘nouthetic counselling’ - which treats addiction as sin, not an illness. Recovery means repentance through punishment, and change - coming from scripture, not science.”

(MASA): “A controversial approach, it emphasises what it calls confrontation. Nowhere, though, does it entertain violence.”

(Donovan de Klerk Facebook video): “Hi, my name is Donovan I am a sinner. That’s not really something you hear everyday. But maybe it should be. I think if we hear that more often, maybe people would recover a lot better.”

(MASA): “Donovan de Klerk is the founder and spiritual leader of Tetelestai. And a former addict.”

(MASA): “He isn’t medically qualified.”
(ANONYMOUS): “A lot of it is prison-style run… soap in sock…Only hit on the body… You know beat you with their hands, or their shoes, or any hard object they can find….”
(MASA): “This is a former Tetelestai counsellor turned whistleblower.”
(ANONYMOUS): “So if you didn’t adhere to the initial punishment, you’d be put on a more severe punishment, which would entail something known as ‘Full Hold’.”
(MASA): “Full hold is a type of punishment. Residents are forced to work from dawn to dusk, using toothbrushes to scrub floors and toilets, and teaspoons to dig one-metre holes – before refilling them.”

(MASA): “No speaking. No rest.”
(MASA): “Apparently Donovan preaches that addiction is a symptom of sin?”
(ANONYMOUS): “That is the auspice under which everything pretty much runs. And then therefore this sin needs to be put off, and God needs to be put on.”
(ANONYMOUS): “You have to follow those specific steps, and he’s the Director and the leader, so you have to follow what he says because what he says is right and it’s according to the Word.”

(MASA): “Former staff say Donovan never gave direct orders, but his intent was clear.”
(ANONYMOUS): “The words won’t necessarily be used like ‘beat him’, there’ll be phrases like ‘do what you need to do, I will, I will have your back’.”
(MASA): “You weren’t surprised to hear about the death of Luke Edwards?”
(ANONYMOUS): “It was only a matter of time. First it’s no medication, then that gets overlooked. Then it’s no food, then that gets overlooked. Then it’s a little beating, then that gets overlooked. So every time something gets overlooked, you know, something worse happens…”


(MASA): “Luke’s family hired private investigator, Brad Nathanson. His leads were crucial in the arrest of the four suspects.”

(BRAD NATHANSON): “I cannot imagine the pain of a family that sees their child in trouble, takes the child to a facility for rehabilitation, and gets the child returned to them in the state that he was returned. It broke my heart.”

(MASA): “He says the accused men admitted to manhandling Luke, but claim it was restraint, not assault.”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “They admitted to cable-tying him. They also come to a point where, where everything just seem to stop. Where no one can tell me what happened from this point onwards.”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “How did he suddenly escape in the middle of the night, and why was it never ever reported to anybody? Why wasn’t it reported to the police? You’ve got a man on psychosis… he’s a danger to himself, he’s a danger to others. He escapes your facility, and you don’t report this case to anybody? You just leave it alone until the next morning at 7 o’ clock?”

(MASA): “Were his parents aware that he was being beaten - and this was also part of their programme?”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “No… There’s an air of violence because of the kind of people that are there. There are psychotic people, there are people going through psychosis; there are members of the Numbers gangs. There is, it sounds to me when I listen to the stories that this is more like a penal colony than it is a rehabilitation centre, and it’s dangerous.”

(MASA): “Brad’s enquiries led to a disturbing conclusion.”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “It became very clear to me that this was not just an isolated incident, but an incident that is of regular occurrence at this Tetelestai Recovery Centre.”
(Donovan de Klerk Facebook video): “The debt that we owe God for these sinful lives we’ve been living has genuinely been paid in full through Christ.”
(MASA): “Donovan de Klerk denies the violence, but these voice notes, sent to us anonymously, tell a different story.

(PATIENT 3 - ANONYMOUS): “Donovan is manipulative, he’s a monster. The punishments, the hiding behind religion to preach your own gospel… it’s not okay.”

(PATIENT 4 - ANONYMOUS): "He kind of pretends to be a man of God, quotes verses from the Bible and everything else, but every second word is an ‘f’ or a ‘c’ or this and that. So it’s complete hypocrisy.”

(PATIENT 5 - ANONYMOUS): “To this day I call it ‘Tetelestai Penitentiary Centre’ - not a recovery centre.”



(MASA): “We’ve heard dozens of accounts from different sources, all claiming what happens at Tetelestai isn’t healing - it’s harm.”

(MASA): “After sending her teenaged daughter there five years ago, this woman says abuse soon followed.”
(ANONYMOUS): “The patients were jumping the wall and escaping, they were forever escaping and running back. A girl lost her life there because of the abuse - she just wanted to go home. My daughter was there with friends and her friends were telling them to please call the ambulance - and they never did. Two weeks later my daughter found out the young girl died.”
(MASA): “How did that affect her? Did she regress?”
(ANONYMOUS): “Still to this day, I as a parent regret sending her there. She hasn’t picked up the pieces… but in fact, it’s destroyed her.”
(MASA): “This mother, Henrene Wilken, also raised concerns. She says Donovan made advances on her daughter-in-law.”
(HENRENE WILKEN): “He got romantically involved with my daughter-in-law. My son paid for her to be in the facility with the hope that it would restore their marriage and the brokenness within their relationship, that that would be a restoration, a moment of healing for them as a family. But we’ve experienced exactly the opposite.”
(MASA): “Not only a concerned mother, Henrene is also a social worker with forty years’ experience.”
(MASA): “From your professional opinion, you know, what does that say?”
(HENRENE WILKEN): “This should never happen - in any organisation - no matter what. You do not punish people. I’ve also heard stories of people having to dig holes and sit in the baking sun outside, and for their punishment. I’ve heard of abuse, water being thrown over people. I’ve heard of people being isolated. That is abuse. You just don’t do that; it’s just not done.”
(MASA): “In June, the four Tetelestai ‘monitors’ were charged with murder.”

(MASA): “De Klerk sat in the public gallery.”

(MASA): “That same afternoon, he was back online - promoting a cryptocurrency exchange.”
(X video): “Oh my bud, we’re gonna cook. The cooking is coming from *bleeped out*. You beautiful biscuits. Legends!”
(MASA): “No mention of Luke.”
(X video): “Legends. That’s all I can say. Thank you, thank you, thank you.”
(MASA): “De Klerk’s lawyer told us he wouldn’t be commenting. But, when he returned to court for the accused’s bail application, we confronted him.”
(MASA): “Donovan, Masa from Carte Blanche. Are you not going to say anything? We’d like to speak to you about Luke Edwards’ death.”
“Have you got nothing to say about the allegations going on at your centre?”
“Torture, abuse, cable-tying, starving patients…?”
“Donovan you’ve got nothing to say?”

(MASA): “The four monitors got bail of R2000 each.”



(LUKE MEMORIAL): “Wherever he is right now, he’s definitely tearing up the dance floor, and being the life of the party. Luke was my best friend, and I loved him so much…”
(BRAD NATHANSON): “Doesn’t matter what goes on with this investigation; we can’t bring Luke back. All we can do is prevent this from happening again.”
(MASA): “Luke’s parents hope for justice while living with grief - and regret.”

(MASA): “I’m going to ask you something that may be really tough right now: if you could say something to your son Luke, what would it be?”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “We’re so sorry we couldn’t protect you.”
(DUNCAN EDWARDS): “That’s all…”
(LINDA EDWARDS): “ If we had known, we would’ve done more.”

(MASA):
“Donovan de Klerk denies any wrongdoing. The case hasn’t closed.
Tetelestai hasn’t either.”’

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 03 August 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Deadly Deliverance A young man in the grip of cannabis-induced psychosis is admitted to a Christian rehab centre on the KwaZulu Natal coast. Days later, his body is found barefoot, shirtless, and beaten so badly, it looks like torture. Witnesses provide shocking accounts, and investigations reveal the centre has no doctors, no therapists, and no psychiatric oversight. What really happened to this young man inside the facility, which promised healing through prayer? His family believes he was murdered… and witnesses claim he’s not the first. Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana Script: DEADLY DELIVERANCE: FINAL (MASA): “It’s early morning in April this year. (MASA): “CCTV footage shows a young man probably disoriented, possibly Injured.” (MASA): “It’s later established that he’s an escapee from a nearby drug rehabilitation centre.” (MASA): “Hours later… Luke Edwards is found dead.” (MASA): “The centre in question promised healing through Christian scripture... but insiders reveal its methods were anything but spiritual.” (PATIENT 1 - ANONYMOUS): “They told us pain was part of the process. That suffering meant we were healing.” (MASA): “Punishment was routine.” (PATIENT 2 - ANONYMOUS): “He uses punishment as a form of - if you abide to this punishment, God will forgive you.” (MASA): “Luke died less than a week after being admitted.” (BRAD NATHANSON): “I can tell that this man was beaten for a long period of time.” (LINDA DAVIDS): “They were beating psychosis out of people… and that’s why he’s dead.” (MASA): “The centre’s name comes from the Bible. Tetelestai means: “It is finished.” (MASA): “For Luke… it was.” (MASA): “Luke had just returned from abroad. He was 32. A writer.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “He was clever, he was artistic, he was passionate about things. He had friends all over the world. He loved like I’ve never seen a boy love.” (MASA): “But, after his return, he became paranoid... agitated. His family was told he was experiencing cannabis-induced psychosis.” (MASA): “Searching for help, they found Tetelestai Recovery Centre in Amanzimtoti, in KZN.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “So we went out to the centre. We had a long meeting with him.” (MASA): “Luke’s parents, Linda and Duncan Edwards, with the founder, Donovan de Klerk.” (MASA): “He assured them Luke would be evaluated by a doctor.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “I said to him: ‘Do you have a psychiatrist or a psychologist on the premises?’; he said no they don’t, but they have a doctor that comes in once a week, and she’ll do a full evaluation; if she feels he needs to go to a psychiatrist, they will.” (MASA): “Reassured, they had Luke admitted.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “He had I think a two-week initial period there where they detox and they're not allowed to see family and that, I said that’s fine. I said after that, I will get my own psychiatrist in there to check on Luke, and he said that wasn’t a problem’.” (MASA): “So it didn’t even get to two weeks?” (LINDA EDWARDS): “No, no, no. Within a, well literally a week, the following Tuesday he was dead.” (MASA): “Tetelestai told the family Luke had escaped the facility the night before he was found.” (MASA): “They didn’t immediately phone the police… or his parents.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “If they had phoned me at 11 o’clock that night, we family would never let Luke wander around at 11 o’clock night…” (DUNCAN EDWARDS): “I still would’ve been there…” (LINDA EDWARDS): “We would’ve been there at 11 o’ clock and maybe we could’ve saved Luke…” (MASA): “Now you were given a version of events by the centre of what had happened initially… Does that information contradict one another?” (LINDA EDWARDS): “Oh absolutely. Absolutely…” (MASA): “Tell me how…?” (LINDA EDWARDS): “They say he absconded, so for me he escaped. From witnesses that have - he was actually pushed ou himself.” (DUNCAN EDWARDS): “Dragged out.” (LINDA EDWARDS): “He was dragged out.” (MASA): “Luke’s lifeless body was found somewhere around here - in the street, just 250 metres away from Tetelestai’s gates.” (MASA): “Four men from the centre were charged with his murder. They weren’t trained staff. Just former addicts who’d finished the programme. Tetelestai called them “monitors.” (MASA): “Were you told about the monitors when you spoke to Donovan initially?” (LINDA EDWARDS): “Nope… As far as we were aware, all his employees had the right qualifications.” (MASA): “Luke’s injuries were extensive: bruises, blunt force trauma, cable tie marks, and a knife wound believed to be fatal.” (DUNCAN EDWARDS): “I went to the morgue. I saw his body. It was the most horrific thing I’ve ever seen in my entire life. Worst day of my life. I went there with my brother-in-laws, and we just all - we were mortified at the condition his body was in. It was, it was mind blowing. Absolutely mind blowing.” (MASA): “What Tetelestai offers isn’t recognised therapy. It’s a religious belief system which is built on a model called ‘nouthetic counselling’ - which treats addiction as sin, not an illness. Recovery means repentance through punishment, and change - coming from scripture, not science.” (MASA): “A controversial approach, it emphasises what it calls confrontation. Nowhere, though, does it entertain violence.” (Donovan de Klerk Facebook video): “Hi, my name is Donovan I am a sinner. That’s not really something you hear everyday. But maybe it should be. I think if we hear that more often, maybe people would recover a lot better.” (MASA): “Donovan de Klerk is the founder and spiritual leader of Tetelestai. And a former addict.” (MASA): “He isn’t medically qualified.” (ANONYMOUS): “A lot of it is prison-style run… soap in sock…Only hit on the body… You know beat you with their hands, or their shoes, or any hard object they can find….” (MASA): “This is a former Tetelestai counsellor turned whistleblower.” (ANONYMOUS): “So if you didn’t adhere to the initial punishment, you’d be put on a more severe punishment, which would entail something known as ‘Full Hold’.” (MASA): “Full hold is a type of punishment. Residents are forced to work from dawn to dusk, using toothbrushes to scrub floors and toilets, and teaspoons to dig one-metre holes – before refilling them.” (MASA): “No speaking. No rest.” (MASA): “Apparently Donovan preaches that addiction is a symptom of sin?” (ANONYMOUS): “That is the auspice under which everything pretty much runs. And then therefore this sin needs to be put off, and God needs to be put on.” (ANONYMOUS): “You have to follow those specific steps, and he’s the Director and the leader, so you have to follow what he says because what he says is right and it’s according to the Word.” (MASA): “Former staff say Donovan never gave direct orders, but his intent was clear.” (ANONYMOUS): “The words won’t necessarily be used like ‘beat him’, there’ll be phrases like ‘do what you need to do, I will, I will have your back’.” (MASA): “You weren’t surprised to hear about the death of Luke Edwards?” (ANONYMOUS): “It was only a matter of time. First it’s no medication, then that gets overlooked. Then it’s no food, then that gets overlooked. Then it’s a little beating, then that gets overlooked. So every time something gets overlooked, you know, something worse happens…” (MASA): “Luke’s family hired private investigator, Brad Nathanson. His leads were crucial in the arrest of the four suspects.” (BRAD NATHANSON): “I cannot imagine the pain of a family that sees their child in trouble, takes the child to a facility for rehabilitation, and gets the child returned to them in the state that he was returned. It broke my heart.” (MASA): “He says the accused men admitted to manhandling Luke, but claim it was restraint, not assault.” (BRAD NATHANSON): “They admitted to cable-tying him. They also come to a point where, where everything just seem to stop. Where no one can tell me what happened from this point onwards.” (BRAD NATHANSON): “How did he suddenly escape in the middle of the night, and why was it never ever reported to anybody? Why wasn’t it reported to the police? You’ve got a man on psychosis… he’s a danger to himself, he’s a danger to others. He escapes your facility, and you don’t report this case to anybody? You just leave it alone until the next morning at 7 o’ clock?” (MASA): “Were his parents aware that he was being beaten - and this was also part of their programme?” (BRAD NATHANSON): “No… There’s an air of violence because of the kind of people that are there. There are psychotic people, there are people going through psychosis; there are members of the Numbers gangs. There is, it sounds to me when I listen to the stories that this is more like a penal colony than it is a rehabilitation centre, and it’s dangerous.” (MASA): “Brad’s enquiries led to a disturbing conclusion.” (BRAD NATHANSON): “It became very clear to me that this was not just an isolated incident, but an incident that is of regular occurrence at this Tetelestai Recovery Centre.” (Donovan de Klerk Facebook video): “The debt that we owe God for these sinful lives we’ve been living has genuinely been paid in full through Christ.” (MASA): “Donovan de Klerk denies the violence, but these voice notes, sent to us anonymously, tell a different story. (PATIENT 3 - ANONYMOUS): “Donovan is manipulative, he’s a monster. The punishments, the hiding behind religion to preach your own gospel… it’s not okay.” (PATIENT 4 - ANONYMOUS): "He kind of pretends to be a man of God, quotes verses from the Bible and everything else, but every second word is an ‘f’ or a ‘c’ or this and that. So it’s complete hypocrisy.” (PATIENT 5 - ANONYMOUS): “To this day I call it ‘Tetelestai Penitentiary Centre’ - not a recovery centre.” (MASA): “We’ve heard dozens of accounts from different sources, all claiming what happens at Tetelestai isn’t healing - it’s harm.” (MASA): “After sending her teenaged daughter there five years ago, this woman says abuse soon followed.” (ANONYMOUS): “The patients were jumping the wall and escaping, they were forever escaping and running back. A girl lost her life there because of the abuse - she just wanted to go home. My daughter was there with friends and her friends were telling them to please call the ambulance - and they never did. Two weeks later my daughter found out the young girl died.” (MASA): “How did that affect her? Did she regress?” (ANONYMOUS): “Still to this day, I as a parent regret sending her there. She hasn’t picked up the pieces… but in fact, it’s destroyed her.” (MASA): “This mother, Henrene Wilken, also raised concerns. She says Donovan made advances on her daughter-in-law.” (HENRENE WILKEN): “He got romantically involved with my daughter-in-law. My son paid for her to be in the facility with the hope that it would restore their marriage and the brokenness within their relationship, that that would be a restoration, a moment of healing for them as a family. But we’ve experienced exactly the opposite.” (MASA): “Not only a concerned mother, Henrene is also a social worker with forty years’ experience.” (MASA): “From your professional opinion, you know, what does that say?” (HENRENE WILKEN): “This should never happen - in any organisation - no matter what. You do not punish people. I’ve also heard stories of people having to dig holes and sit in the baking sun outside, and for their punishment. I’ve heard of abuse, water being thrown over people. I’ve heard of people being isolated. That is abuse. You just don’t do that; it’s just not done.” (MASA): “In June, the four Tetelestai ‘monitors’ were charged with murder.” (MASA): “De Klerk sat in the public gallery.” (MASA): “That same afternoon, he was back online - promoting a cryptocurrency exchange.” (X video): “Oh my bud, we’re gonna cook. The cooking is coming from *bleeped out*. You beautiful biscuits. Legends!” (MASA): “No mention of Luke.” (X video): “Legends. That’s all I can say. Thank you, thank you, thank you.” (MASA): “De Klerk’s lawyer told us he wouldn’t be commenting. But, when he returned to court for the accused’s bail application, we confronted him.” (MASA): “Donovan, Masa from Carte Blanche. Are you not going to say anything? We’d like to speak to you about Luke Edwards’ death.” “Have you got nothing to say about the allegations going on at your centre?” “Torture, abuse, cable-tying, starving patients…?” “Donovan you’ve got nothing to say?” (MASA): “The four monitors got bail of R2000 each.” (LUKE MEMORIAL): “Wherever he is right now, he’s definitely tearing up the dance floor, and being the life of the party. Luke was my best friend, and I loved him so much…” (BRAD NATHANSON): “Doesn’t matter what goes on with this investigation; we can’t bring Luke back. All we can do is prevent this from happening again.” (MASA): “Luke’s parents hope for justice while living with grief - and regret.” (MASA): “I’m going to ask you something that may be really tough right now: if you could say something to your son Luke, what would it be?” (LINDA EDWARDS): “We’re so sorry we couldn’t protect you.” (DUNCAN EDWARDS): “That’s all…” (LINDA EDWARDS): “ If we had known, we would’ve done more.” (MASA): “Donovan de Klerk denies any wrongdoing. The case hasn’t closed. Tetelestai hasn’t either.”’

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): He went in for healing. He left in a body bag.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We investigate a Christian recovery centre where the Bible is weaponised against addicts seeking rehabilitation and repentance.
metadata.Summary: Luke Edwards was 32. A writer. A chess player. A son. And in the grip of a cannabis-induced psychosis in April this year when his family made the call: send him to a Christian rehab centre on the KZN South Coast - a place that promised healing through prayer. Nine days later, Luke’s body was found - barefoot, shirtless, and dumped in the bushes (in full display for the world to see) near a retirement home. He’d been beaten so badly, investigators said it looked like torture. The Tetelestai Recovery Centre said he’d “absconded.” But CCTV tells another story… Hours after his supposed escape, Luke is caught on camera - fully clothed, calm, coherent, and very much alive. Witnesses say he was cable-tied, locked in a holding cell at the facility, and beaten for days by so-called “monitors” - ex-addicts turned enforcers. Not staff. Not trained. Just violent men recruited for muscle, not mercy. And the facility? No doctors. No therapists. No psychiatric oversight. Just scripture, fear, and fists. TRC’s founder, Donovan de Klerk, once hailed as a “_Young Mandela_,” now faces a different spotlight. Since Luke’s death: - Four residents have been charged with murder (as of yesterday). - Three staff members face assault and intimidation charges. - One resident has died by suicide (a week after Luke’s death). - Another was hospitalised and is in ICU after allegedly being beaten for defending a witness. According to Luke’s family, this wasn’t recovery, this was murder. Luke Edwards is one name, but witnesses say he’s not the first.
metadata.Further information: We investigate a Christian rehab centre where salvation came at the end of a fist, and how South Africa’s faith-based facilities are operating in the shadows, trading therapy for theology, and with no rules, no oversight, and no accountability. And we expose what really happened in the final hours of Luke Edwards’ life - through the eyes of witnesses, a veteran PI hired by his grieving family to uncover the truth; and CCTV footage.
